message.abstract: <jats:p>The service life of most load-bearing steel components is governed by fatigue failure, while direct fatigue-strength measurement remains costly and time-consuming. In this study, regression models are developed and benchmarked for predicting the rotating-bending fatigue strength of steels using heat-treatment parameters, chemical composition, and inclusion metrics from the National Institute for Materials Science fatigue dataset. Under nested cross-validation with all preprocessing confined to training folds, gradient-boosted trees and support-vector regression are identified as the leading models, with Extreme Gradient Boosting selected as the final predictive model. Model transparency is established through explainable methods, including Shapley Additive Explanations, partial dependence, individual conditional expectation, accumulated local effects, variance-based Sobol indices, and permutation importance. Fatigue strength is attributed primarily to normalizing temperature, chromium content, and tempering temperature, while established metallurgical mechanisms and a dominant interaction between normalizing temperature and chromium content are recovered without prior physical input. Distribution-free, regime-conditional conformal prediction intervals are further incorporated to quantify predictive uncertainty. Generalization beyond the sampled steel-grade envelope is additionally quantified through a grouped, leave-one-grade-out evaluation. A reliability-aware design framework is introduced in which process and composition parameters are optimized according to a conformally calibrated lower-bound fatigue strength, carrying finite-sample marginal coverage, rather than point predictions. Overall, accurate, interpretable, and risk-bounded machine learning is demonstrated as a trustworthy approach for accelerating steel alloy and process design.</jats:p>
title: From Explainable Predictions to Reliability-Aware Design: Interpretable Machine Learning for the Fatigue Strength of Steels
